The quiet comeback of the night train

By Ingrid Solberg · 7 min read

Fifteen years ago Europe's sleeper trains looked finished. Budget airlines had taken their passengers, operators had sold off their carriages, and one route after another made its last run. Today the map is filling in again, and the trains are often sold out weeks ahead.

The revival started with Austria's state railway, which bought several night lines that others had abandoned in 2016. Instead of treating them as a nostalgic loss-maker, it ran them as a product: clear prices, online booking, and new carriages with small private sleeping pods for people who did not want to share a compartment with strangers.

Demand followed. Travellers who wanted to cut their flying found that a sleeper turns a full travel day into a night's sleep. A trip from Vienna to Amsterdam leaves after dinner and arrives in time for breakfast, which no daytime train can match and which compares well with an early flight plus the airport transfers on both ends.

Problems remain. Night trains need staff on board all night, they use expensive rolling stock for only one trip per day, and track access fees in several countries are charged as if they were ordinary passenger trains. Operators say those fees can make up a third of the ticket price. Border crossings add delays when crews and locomotives have to change.

Several governments now treat sleepers as climate policy rather than a niche. Sweden pays for overnight services to Germany, France has restored lines from Paris to the Alps and the Mediterranean, and the European Commission has proposed easing cross-border rules. Whether the comeback lasts depends less on nostalgia than on those unglamorous details: fees, staff, and enough beds to sell.
